Elliott Whitney writes a big-game hunt for boys in the Boys' Big Game Series. A party sets out with wagons, water casks, and guides, chasing a rogue elephant through strange country. Captain Yonge and von Hofe lead the march, while a native runner brings news of an outbreak fifty miles west. The commissioner saddles in haste to quash a riot, leaving the hunters to push on.

Cold nights at high altitude disgust the boys, who were hardly prepared for cold in that region. Day and night they force the march through valleys and slopes toward their quarry. Reilly and Britton published the book at Chicago in 1913, illustrated by Fred J. Arting, with a cover by Dan Sayre Groesbeck.
25463-the-day-of-judgment:
Joseph Hocking's 1915 novel follows Paul through a legacy of hate toward a day of judgment. Chapters trace Paul's work, his prison term, his meeting with Mary Bolitho, and his madness. He goes to Scotland, fights, and faces his mother's coming, a seat for Brunford, and a night of doom. At last he is apprehended for murder, hears the coroner's inquest, and awaits trial.

Paul's private torment centers on Mary: he believes he can save her from Wilson, if only he can prove what he knows. Yet proof would make him look a spy and an informer, striking below the belt. He trudges the road repeating that she must know the truth, and that he will not be beaten. Cassell published the novel in London, New York, Toronto, and Melbourne.
25885-all-the-brothers-were-valiant:
Ben Ames Williams sets a sea tale of kin, courage, and dark deeds around a fine old house on Jumping Tom Hill. The house stood before the town, its boards shipped ready sawn from England, and Indians once begged shelter there in winter cold, sleeping on the kitchen floor. Joel Shore, heir to that house, watches his brothers go to sea and come home changed.

Printed in 1919, the novel follows Mark Shore to a far island, where a pearling schooner waits for a rival to leave so its crew can take brown women as companions. Mark, rifle in arm and a small brown girl at his heel, makes a treaty on deck. The book weighs what valor costs when brothers choose different paths, and how a house and a name bear the weight.
26477-observations-on-the-florid-song-or:
Pier Francesco Tosi, of the Phil-Harmonic Academy at Bologna, wrote this treatise on florid song in Italian in 1723, and Mr. Galliard translated it into English for London publication in 1743. Tosi compares ancient singers, meaning those of thirty or forty years before, with modern singers, and argues that vocal music holds preeminence over instrumental music by nature and art. The voice, he holds, expresses sounds with greater nicety than any instrument.

The book serves performers vocal and instrumental alike, with explanatory annotations and examples in music. Tosi warns singers against parading all their talent in a few songs, lest they go bankrupt of effects, and he insists that pains in studying airs can never be too great. The treatise remains a classic guide to Baroque singing style.
26626-our-little-brown-house-a-poem-of-w:
Maria L. Stewart, signing herself M. L. S., published this poem at New York in 1880, after reading it at the New Year's festival of the Cadets' Sabbath School of the Methodist Episcopal Church on January 1, 1879. Her preface says the poems were meant only to interest the Sabbath school, and friends urged her to print them. The title poem honors a little brown chapel under the hill at West Point.

Built from the gun-house of Colonel Thayer's fame, the small plain house was altered again and again by captains and colonels, with doors moved, roofs changed, and stoves replaced. Stewart then turns to the loved ones met there of yore, now scattered from the Missouri falls to the Pacific slopes and the Atlantic coast. Some married, some died, and some face frontier war, but all live in the chapel's memory.
26707-wanderings-in-the-orient:
Albert M. Reese published this travel diary with the Open Court Publishing Company at Chicago and London in 1919, with sixty-six illustrations from his own photographs. Reese argues that Americans, for whom going abroad usually means Europe, should turn to the Far East while European travel stays unsatisfactory. Cook, he notes, is nearly always ready to help the traveler out of difficulties.

Reese sailed on the army transport Sherman, twenty-eight days from San Francisco to Manila, as a Smithsonian representative, and made Manila his headquarters for collecting trips. Chapters cover life in a Philippine village, Tay Tay, and the leper colony of Culion. They continue from Zamboanga to Singapore, Singapore as melting pot of the East, and how rubber is made. Two Chinese cities, modern Manila, and Honolulu as a Pacific paradise close the book. Mariveles village lies inside the cape at Manila Bay's entrance, under Corregidor's searchlights.
26767-notes-and-queries-number-208-octob:
This number of Notes and Queries, number 208, dated Saturday, October 22, 1853, priced at fourpence, calls itself a medium of inter-communication for literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists. Its motto, from Captain Cuttle, is When found, make a note of. Notes, queries, replies, and miscellaneous matter fill pages 381 to 402.

Notes open with a prophet, Thomas Newans, a Shropshire farmer who fancied his visit to the lower sphere had a special mission. Folk lore follows from Cambridgeshire, New Brunswick, North Lincolnshire, and Portugal, with Pope and Cowper and Shakespeare correspondence. Queries ask about Sir Thomas Button's voyage of 1612, the words cash and mob, Napoleon's spelling, and where Edward the Second was killed. Replies treat Namby Pamby, Picts' houses, and the pronunciation of humble.
26858-crossing-the-plains-days-of-57-a-n:
Wm. Audley Maxwell wrote this narrative of emigrant travel to California by the ox-team method, published by Sunset Publishing House in San Francisco in 1915. His company left the west bank of the Missouri on May 17, 1857, bound for Sonoma County. Thirty-seven people made the party: eleven men, ten women, and sixteen children. They took eight wagons, about thirty yoke of oxen, and fifty extra steers. The eldest was forty-nine; the youngest, a boy two months old.

Thirteen chapters carry the train past Chimney Rock and Devil's Gate, through the Black Hills and a tornado, to the Holloway Massacre, disaster for the Wood family, and sagebrush justice. Maxwell warns that the four hundred miles down the Humboldt, from Thousand Springs to the settlements, would take nearly a month and prove the most desert-like stretch of the whole trip. Illustrations mark the fords, the stampedes, and the camp routines.
27006-notes-and-queries-number-207-octob:
Notes and Queries number 207, for October 15, 1853, leads with notes on Midland county minstrelsy by C. Clifton Barry, comet superstitions in 1853, and the old English word Belike. T. J. Buckton writes on the Druses, and folk lore from County Clare continues.

Shakespeare correspondence and a note on death on the fingers fill the middle pages, with minor notes on a custom of the English and epitaphs at Crayford. Queries ask after Lovett of Astwell, oaths, and the electric telegraph, showing the weekly tracking both old customs and new inventions. Minor notes add an epitaph at Crayford and the font at Islip, and queries also ask about Lord Ball of Bagshot and the claymore.
27007-notes-and-queries-number-210-novem:
For Saturday, November 5, 1853, Notes and Queries number 210 leads with Professor De Morgan on Lord Halifax and Mrs. Catherine Barton, followed by Dr. Parr on Milton and notes on William Blake. Folk lore from County Clare tells of the Seven Whisperers.

Minor notes range from decomposed cloth and cucumber time to stage coaches, Boswell's Johnson, and the letter X. Queries ask after bishops, mottoes, bees, and Nelly O'Brien and Kitty Fisher. A note on parts of manuscripts by John Macray sits among the contents, keeping the weekly's mix of scholarship and small mystery intact.
27011-notes-and-queries-number-214-decem:
December 3, 1853 brings Notes and Queries number 214, with notes on Peter Brett, Richard's Guide through France, women and tortoises, and weather rules by W. Winthrop. Occasional forms of prayer get a full note from Reverend Thomas Lathbury.

Minor notes run from an epitaph on Politian in Florence to the early delights of Philadelphia and an ancient gold collar found in Staffordshire. Queries seek pictures in Hampton Court Palace, the will of Peter the Great, and a manuscript by Rubens, among other antiquarian wants. A minor note records a chair moving and Plantin Bibles in 1600, and the number is priced fourpence, fivepence stamped.
27072-the-flying-doctor-le-me-decin-vola:
Molière's The Flying Doctor, Le Médecin Volant, was first acted in Paris on April 18, 1659, and parts of it later reappeared in L'Amour Médecin and Le Médecin malgré lui. Molière himself played Sganarelle, servant to Valère.

The plot turns on a device to stop a forced marriage: Lucile, whom her father Gorgibus would marry to Villebrequin, affects illness, while her cousin Sabine fetches a doctor. Valère's man Sganarelle must play the doctor and order country air, so the lovers can meet in the garden pavilion unseen.
27103-the-little-russian-servant:
Henri Greville's The Little Russian Servant, issued as Neely's Booklet number 24 in June 1899, opens with a countess inspecting a new girl of fifteen or sixteen. The girl, daughter of Foma of the village of Ikonine, has come to pay her father's obrok while he is in Moscow.

The head lady's maid, thirty years in service, vouches for the girl's embroidery, fit for trimmings if not for the ground. The short-sharp countess, short-sighted from birth, peers until her nose grazes the cloth. Greville's tale gives a glimpse of serf-era Russia through a servant girl's first days.
2717-nona-vincent:
Henry James wrote this short tale of a writer and the woman who asks him to read his work aloud. Mrs. Alsager lingers by the fire, drawing her dress away from the flames, and asks with shy sincerity whether he would read it to her.

Her charm, always great, grows as the reading reveals a play, a past, and feelings neither can quite name. James writes with his usual tact, letting silence carry what speech cannot. The tale charms as a study of art, admiration, and the tender danger of being understood too well.
27211-jerry-s-charge-account:
Hazel Wilson's Jerry's Charge Account, published by Little, Brown in 1960 with illustrations by Charles Geer, follows Jerry Martin into trouble over candy. When the sweets in Mr. Bartlett's store prove too tempting, Jerry starts the charge account and its worry.

Keeping his twin sister Cathy guessing and his secret from the family, especially little brother Andy, proves sort of fun, until Jerry sinks like a man in quicksand. His father disapproves of charge accounts, and a break-in at Mr. Bullfinch's house next door turns fun serious, with laughter, suspense, and a hidden lesson.
27233-the-critic-in-the-orient:
George Hamlin Fitch's The Critic in the Orient, published by Paul Elder in 1913, collects chapters first printed in the Sunday supplement of the San Francisco Chronicle. A Kipling epigraph opens the book, and the frontispiece shows the Taj Mahal at Agra, matchless in form and symmetry.

Fitch's travels reach the Philippines, where the Constabulary Guard, with American officers and young college graduates as captains, polices districts like Mexican rurales or Canadian mounted police. The critic writes as counselor and friend to readers meeting the East through books, buildings, and peoples.
27485-the-critics-versus-shakspere-a-bri:
Francis A. Smith, of counsel, published this brief for the defendant with the Knickerbocker Press in New York in 1907. Smith casts three centuries of Shakespeare criticism as a lawsuit, The Critics Against Shakspere, in which he was retained long ago. The case has been decided, reopened, and reheard again and again.

Each time, Smith says, the most eminent judges non-suited the plaintiffs. Appeals failed, and the great jury of mankind returned a verdict of no cause of action. Ben Jonson charged that Shakspere wanted art, yet Lear was judged greater than anything by Euripides or Sophocles. Smith defends the poet with lawyerly wit.
27643-lucile-triumphant:
Elizabeth M. Duffield, author of Lucile on the Heights and Lucile, Bringer of Joy, published this Lucile story with the Whitman Publishing Company of Racine, Wisconsin, in 1916. It follows the heroine of her earlier books into new travels.

The great news breaks at once: Europe. Two girls regard their companion in open-mouthed astonishment as Jessie cries out the word. Chapters run from greetings, fellow-travelers, and echoes of the camp-fire through a latter-day miracle, the magic city, and enter Jack, to hurrah for Europe and whirled through the night. A red-letter day, the old chateau, and the heart of the mystery lead to Lucile triumphant.
27665-junior-achievement:
William Lee wrote this short science-fiction story about Donald, a junior high science teacher in the town of Ridgeville, who agrees to lead a junior achievement group for the summer. The group teaches schoolchildren about commerce by making and selling simple products such as polishing wax.

Told with gentle humor, the story follows Donald's doubts about his own business sense as the children take the project seriously. It ends up being a warm tale about teaching, small enterprise, and a teacher learning from his pupils. Donald teaches general science at the junior high and physics at the senior high school.
27737-le-petit-chose-histoire-d-un-enfan:
Alphonse Daudet's Le Petit Chose, subtitled Histoire d'un enfant, appears here in a school edition adapted and edited by S. Tindall for Macmillan's Siepmann's Advanced French Series. The 1921 printing presents the first part, Le Petit Chose en province, with notes and study aids.

The novel follows a boy, the little fellow of the title, through childhood in provincial France, told in Daudet's warm and lightly comic voice. Questionnaires, word lists, and writing topics in the appendices mark this as a classroom text, meant to teach French through a story students could enjoy.
27797-vital-ingredient:
Gerald Vance wrote this short science-fiction story about Frankie, a boxer ready for the big test as ten-time winner of the world title. Frankie has youth, fitness, and ability, plus the cunning brain of Milt directing every feint and punch by mental control.

Frankie waits for his heels to set and for Milt to send power up his legs, but Milt holds back. Frankie begins to doubt the veteran's control. The story asks whether a fighter who has never thrown a punch of his own can own his victory, and it ends on the tension of a last fight.
2784-colonel-starbottle-s-client:
Bret Harte gathers stories in this volume, led by Colonel Starbottle's Client, a tale of the old lawyer's habit of championing lost causes. The postmistress of Laurel Run, a night at Hays Johnson's, and an old woman follow, with a new assistant at Pine Clearing School.

In a pioneer restaurant, a treasure of the galleon, and the ghosts of Stukeley Castle round out the set. Harte writes with his late ease, mixing California and eastern scenes. The volume shows his veteran skill at turning a client, a letter, or a ghost into a story.
2792-my-ten-years-imprisonment:
Silvio Pellico wrote this memoir of ten years' imprisonment, translated from the Italian by Thomas Roscoe in the 1886 Cassell edition. Pellico, an Italian patriot, was arrested by the Austrians for his part in the movement for Italian freedom.

His years in Spielberg fortress, with chains, silence, and fellow prisoners, broke his health but not his spirit. Pellico writes with humility and faith, turning suffering into a testament of endurance. The book became a classic of prison literature, and a voice for Italy's cause. Pellico's chains could not silence his faith or his pen.
27969-the-county-regiment:
Dudley Landon Vaill wrote The County Regiment, a sketch of the Second Regiment of Connecticut Volunteer Heavy Artillery, in the Civil War, published in 1908 under the Litchfield County University Club. The volume opens with a frontispiece of Governor Buckingham.

Illustrations follow the presentation of colors in September 1862, the first encampment in Virginia, Fort Ellsworth, and the first battle, with portraits of colonels Wessells, Kellogg, Mackenzie, and Hubbard. Vaill commemorates Litchfield County's organized effort for national defense, and the book is a local regimental history of lasting value. The book keeps the names and deeds of the men of the county before the reader.
27993-bruin-the-grand-bear-hunt:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote Bruin, the grand bear hunt, following two teenage brothers, sons of a Russian nobleman, who ask to travel the world. Their father agrees on two conditions: bring back well-kept skins of every kind of bear, and travel east to west or west to east without doubling back.

With an old retired guardsman, Pouchskin, the boys travel westward through Europe and beyond, gathering bear trophies and returning home as heroes. The story opens at the Palace Grodonoff on the Neva, with a bear on its coat of arms and two live bears in the courtyard.
27998-the-new-tenant:
E. Phillips Oppenheim wrote The New Tenant, published in New York in 1910 with copyright by C. H. Doscher and Company. The novel opens at Thurwell Court by Thurwell-on-the-Sea on an early morning, with dew on terraced lawns and peacocks on the grey stone balcony.

Chapters follow Falcon's Nest, a murder near it, Mr. Bernard Brown, Helen Thurwell's suspicions, a cheque for one thousand pounds, an arrest, and a trial. Oppenheim's mystery of country houses, jewels, and private agents shows the popular thriller writer building suspense through a long chain of clues.
28149-her-ladyship-s-elephant:
David Dwight Wells wrote Her Ladyship's Elephant, first published in May 1898, as a comic novel founded, he insists, on fact. The elephant itself, acquired by a consul during diplomatic service abroad, is the one impossible figure Wells claims is true. The human characters, he says, are only composite portraits, drawn from many real people.

The story follows Harold Stanley Malcolm St. Hubart Scarsdale of The Towers, Sussex, a young man in new patent boots, as an elephant upsets his household and his plans. Breakfast tables, drawing rooms, and English manners all bend before the beast. Wells tells the farce with a straight face, and the joke grows from the clash of empire and home.
28386-ulysses-s-grant:
Walter Allen wrote Ulysses S. Grant in 1901 for the Riverside Biographical Series, a short life of about one hundred pages with a photogravure portrait. Allen follows Grant from ancestry and youth, through love and war, years of dormant power, and the summons of patriotism, to Springfield, Fort Donelson, Shiloh, Corinth, and Vicksburg. Houghton, Mifflin and Company published the volume.

Later chapters cover Chattanooga, lieutenant-general command, the Wilderness, Richmond, Washington politics, two administrations, a world tour, and reverses of fortune. Allen writes plainly for school readers. The book offers a compact, readable life of America's general and president.
28405-notes-and-queries-number-223-febru:
February 1854 opened in Notes and Queries with number 223, dated Saturday, February 4, still priced at fourpence. The weekly journal served literary men, artists, antiquaries, and genealogists, under Captain Cuttle's motto: When found, make a note of it. Readers sent in notes, asked questions, and answered each other's queries.

Notes here include Dryden on Shakespeare, party similes of the seventeenth century, and the Dutch East India Company. Queries ask about contributors to Knight's Quarterly Magazine and the Stationers' Company. Replies, minor queries with answers, and photographic correspondence on multiplying negatives round out another busy number.
28443-the-readjustment:
Will Irwin's The Readjustment, published in 1910, opens on a California ranch at apricot-picking time. Judge Tiffany, a vigorous old man, leans lightly on his younger wife as they walk down a dusty lane to the orchard. There, twenty women and girls slice fruit at long tables.

Their daughter Eleanor has come back from the city. The novel follows her deliberate choice of ranch life over travel and society, and her parents' worry over how long she will stay content. Irwin writes a quiet novel of family, work, and values, asking what readjustment costs when a young woman chooses a life her parents did not plan for her.
28466-a-catalogue-of-play-equipment:
Jean Lee Hunt compiled A Catalogue of Play Equipment for the Bureau of Educational Experiments in New York in 1918, priced at thirty-five cents as Bulletin Number Eight. It argues that playground apparatus should encourage creative play as well as exercise, and must appeal strongly to a child's imagination.

Outdoor furnishings are judged by safety, durability, sound materials, and careful construction, and by whether they suit solitary play or groups. The catalogue shows city yards, an outdoor laboratory of bricks, boards, and tools, and pieces such as the see-saw, with notes on building them. It remains a charming guide to progressive ideas about children's play.
285-the-lost-continent:
C. J. Cutliffe Hyne's Lost Continent retells the fall of Atlantis through a survivor's memory. The prefatory legatees of Deucalion frame a tale that opens with two stiff sleepers on Grand Canary ground. From there the narrator recalls a return to Atlantis.

Chapters follow a rival navy, the welcome of Phorenice, Zaemon's curse, and the biters of the city walls. A preacher from the mountains, a drugged moon rite, and a buried-alive princess raise the stakes. Siege and storm end the sacred mountain's reign. Hyne's romance mixes myth, adventure, and doom.
28572-letters-on-an-elk-hunt:
Elinore Pruitt Stewart's Letters on an Elk Hunt, copyrighted in 1915, is told in letters by a woman homesteader in Wyoming. Writing to a friend, Stewart describes Green River, where she meets Connie Willis. Connie is a tiny dishwasher who stands on a box to reach the sink, and charms everyone with her rich, mellow voice.

Later letters follow the start of the hunt, Eden Valley, Crazy Olaf, Danyul and his mother, and Elizabeth's romance. They go on to an Indian camp, tooth-hunters, a stampede, and the memory-bed. Stewart writes with humour and first-hand knowledge of frontier life, giving readers a woman's view of homesteading, hunting, and Wyoming neighbours.
28831-key-notes-of-american-liberty-comp:
This 1866 anthology gathers the most important speeches, proclamations, and acts of Congress from the founding of the American government to its own time. A flag history by a noted historian stands beside them. Published by E. B. Treat in New York, it appeals in its preface to the patriotic sentiments of all classes, promising words of burning eloquence that lit the fires of the Revolution.

Inside, readers find the speeches that stirred fathers to battle for independence. They also find the wisdom that steered the ship of state through strife into peace, and the proclamations that guided the country in critical hours. The book is a patriotic reader, not a history, meant to be read with gratitude and pride. It offers a post-Civil War view of the nation's founding words, illustrated throughout.
28964-crumps-the-plain-story-of-a-canadi:
Louis Keene, a captain in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, wrote this 1917 account, Crumps: The Plain Story of a Canadian Who Went, published by Houghton Mifflin. General Leonard Wood's prefatory note praises it as a young officer's path from training to combat. It follows an artist who becomes an expert machine-gun officer. Keene covers training at home and abroad and work at the front.

Wood argues the book should teach Americans the cost of unpreparedness, and the disadvantage of partly equipped troops facing highly organized ones. It also celebrates a shared imperial spirit joining Canada, Britain, and the far colonies behind a just cause. Readers get a direct, modest war memoir, illustrated by the author, from the first years of the Great War.
28999-daisy-s-aunt:
E. F. Benson wrote this novel, Daisy's Aunt, first published in May 1910 by Thomas Nelson and Sons in London, Edinburgh, Dublin, Leeds, and New York. The book opens with Daisy Hanbury poking her parasol between the bars of a tiger's cage, meaning to scratch the tiger's back. The tiger, not knowing her kind intent, savagely bites the end off, with diabolical snarlings.

Daisy turns to her cousin with glowing pleasure, calling the beast a darling. That opening sets the tone: a high-spirited young woman, a watchful aunt, and the social comedy of Edwardian England. Benson, also known for The Princess Sophia, blends faithful realism with poetic romance. Readers get a lively novel of youth, family, and the surprises of a first season.
29151-telepathy-genuine-and-fraudulent:
W. W. Baggally, a member of the council of the Society for Psychical Research, published this book in London in 1917, with a preface by Sir Oliver Lodge. Baggally, an experienced investigator of supernormal phenomena, sets out to separate real telepathy from trickery. Lodge commends the book as the record of a careful investigator.

Part one treats genuine telepathy, part two fraudulent telepathy, and part three the Zancigs, famous mind-reading performers. Baggally also exposes a blindfold trick: a yogi's plaster pads that shifted to allow clear vision with one eye. Readers get a skeptical investigator's guide to mind reading, fair to evidence and sharp about fraud.
29226-the-fall-of-british-tyranny-or-ame:
John Leacock published this play in Philadelphia in 1776, under the full title The Fall of British Tyranny, or American Liberty Triumphant. Leacock remains an elusive figure: his name appears as Leacock, Lacock, and Laycock, and little certain information about him survives. The play's first campaign was planned, the title page says, at the Royal Theatrum Pandemonium at St. James's.

Its cast brings the Goddess of Liberty on stage with Generals Washington, Lee, and Putnam, and a prologue to set the patriotic case. Leacock wrote with good humor, one old account says, and the play cheers American liberty against British rule. Readers get a Revolutionary propaganda play, lively and direct, from the year of independence itself.
29586-the-story-of-the-cotton-plant:
Frederick Wilkinson, director of the Textile and Engineering School at Bolton and co-author of Elements of Cotton Spinning, wrote this story of the cotton plant. It stands in the Library of Useful Stories, printed in 1912 by D. Appleton and Company. Its frontispiece shows a cotton field in Texas, plants bearing mature pods with ripe fibre and seed, and thirty-eight pictures illustrate the text.

Wilkinson gathered facts from many books, among them Baines on cotton manufacture, French on Samuel Crompton, and reports of the United States Agricultural Department. The book follows cotton from field to fibre to cloth. Readers of industrial and plant history will find a clear, well-illustrated primer on a crop that shaped the modern world.
29795-an-ode-read-august-15-1907-at-the-:
Madison Cawein wrote this ode for the dedication of a monument at Gloucester, Massachusetts, on August 15, 1907. The monument marks the founding of the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1623. John P. Morton and Company of Louisville printed the ode in MCMVIII. In Cawein's verses, the founders appear as men who held fast to their rights amid storm and stress, following paths that God had shown them.

Here, the ode says, they laid the corner-stone of freedom and lit the lights of liberty alone. They conquered the wilderness, secured their rights, and hallowed the soil with their blood each day. Toil and sweat of brawn and brain raised them from mere men to giants. The poem is a formal, patriotic ode, meant to be read aloud at a public rite of memory.
29984-the-history-of-the-first-west-indi:
A. B. Ellis, major of the First West India Regiment, wrote The History of the First West India Regiment, printed in London in 1885 by Chapman and Hall. Ellis had already written West African Islands and The Land of Fetish.

An introductory chapter opens the history, and twenty-four chapters follow the regiment's wars. Briar Creek and Stono Ferry in 1779, the sieges of Savannah in 1779 and Charlestown in 1780, and Hobkerk's Hill in 1781 come first. The relief of Ninety-Six and Eutaw Springs in 1781 lead to removal to the West Indies. The expedition to Martinique in 1793, the capture of Martinique, St. Lucia, and Guadeloupe in 1794, and the defence of Fort Matilda follow, with Malcolm's Royal Rangers and the evacuation of St. Lucia in 1795.
30130-due-south-or-cuba-past-and-present:
Maturin M. Ballou gives notes of a voyage to the tropics and a sojourn in Cuba during the last winter. The volume was suggested by his earlier Due West, or Round the World in Ten Months. Houghton, Mifflin published the Boston and New York book in 1885, in an eleventh impression from the Riverside Press at Cambridge. Ballou, a popular travel writer of his day, writes for readers who want Cuba past and present in one readable volume.

The preface presents the book as personal notes rather than a formal history, gathered on the spot during a winter stay. Readers will find the island's towns, people, climate, and customs as a nineteenth-century American traveler saw them, with the past recalled beside the present. As a period travel book, it now serves both as a guide to old Cuba and as a record of how visitors viewed it.
30231-the-vote-that-made-the-president:
David Dudley Field explains the vote that made the president in a short Appleton volume from New York in 1877, on the disputed election that put Rutherford B. Hayes in the White House. At ten minutes past four on the second morning of March 1877, the president of the Senate, before both houses of Congress, announced the electoral count. Of 369 electors appointed, a majority stood at 185, with Hayes of Ohio holding 185 votes and Samuel J. Tilden of New York holding 184.

Hayes was therefore declared elected for four years from March 4, 1877, by a majority of one, under an act of Congress approved January 29, 1877. Field shows how thin the margin ran: one vote shifted to Tilden would have given Tilden the 185, while one vote rejected outright would have left each man at 184. The pamphlet gives a lawyer's clear account of a constitutional crisis settled by counting.
30269-my-autobiography-a-fragment:
F. Max Müller, professor and privy councillor, tells his own life in a fragment published by Scribner's Sons in 1901, with portraits throughout. After the second volume of Auld Lang Syne in 1899, friends pressed him for more than recollections of others: they wanted the springs, aspirations, struggles, failures, and achievements of his own life. Müller answers with chapters on childhood at Dessau, school days at Leipzig, university, Paris, and arrival in England.

Early days and early friends at Oxford follow, closing with a confession, an index, and portraits of Müller aged four, fourteen, twenty, and thirty, plus his father and mother. The fragment stops short of a full life, as its title warns, but it gives a scholar's youth and formation in his own voice. Readers of Victorian learning will find a warm, candid self-portrait.
30373-life-and-literature-over-two-thous:
J. Purver Richardson gathers over two thousand extracts from ancient and modern writers, classified in alphabetical order and copyrighted in 1910. The book is dedicated to his children John Purver and Annie Sue. It runs from letter A through letter Z, with an index, and opens with a note on abilities needing opportunity, a patron, and praise.

Readers can dip into short passages on many topics, arranged so a theme can be found at once rather than read straight through. Richardson presents the collection as a storehouse for speakers, writers, and general readers who want a striking line or a wise sentence at hand. The volume works as a commonplace book for daily browsing.
30416-waste-not-want:
Dave Dryfoos writes a science fiction story about Fred Lubway, eighty-six, who wakes in panic in a strange room. A black imp of panic nudges him at dawn, and he stares at the blank space where Tillie's gray head should have been.

Tillie died in a crash well over a year earlier, and Fred scolds himself for still searching for her each morning. He has never made allowance for his own weakness and does not propose to start now. Yet orientation comes slowly in unfamiliar surroundings. Dryfoos frames a tale of grief, age, and a future ruled by supply, demand, and forced consumption.
30491-vital-ingredient:
Charles V. De Vet opens a science fiction story with a riddle: a thing no living creature can exist without, yet when given to Orville, it killed him. The answer points to a single letter and a single element, teased in the opening note.

Remm shows Macker a captured native, a hunched biped in bright artificial skin, resting on a packing box inside the ship. Macker had missed the capture and the tests, having explored the countryside near the landing place. Its stubby feet, thin pipelike legs, and pallid flesh puzzle the crew. De Vet turns a first contact scene into a puzzle about life, need, and harm.
3050-notes-of-a-war-correspondent:
Richard Harding Davis wrote Notes of a War Correspondent from his reporting across four wars, in the 1911 Scribner edition. Contents cover the Cuban-Spanish War, the death of Rodriguez, and the Greek-Turkish War at Velestinos. The Spanish-American War brings the Rough Riders at Guasimas and San Juan Hill, and the South African War brings Buller's column and the relief of Ladysmith. Davis reported from the firing line. His battle scenes name the dead plainly, from Captain O'Neill of the Rough Riders.

O'Neill said no Spanish bullet could kill him, yet men fell from their saddles to sharpshooters hidden above streams and trails. Bullets came from every side, with invisible smoke to hide the shooters. The book remains a classic of war reporting, vivid, personal, and unsparing.
30531-a-vindication-of-the-seventh-day-s:
Joseph Bates writes A Vindication of the Seventh-Day Sabbath and the Commandments of God. With a further history of God's peculiar people from 1847 to 1848, it was printed in New Bedford in 1848 by Benjamin Lindsey. Bates versifies the ten commandments in his opening, from no God but me thou shalt adore to nor covet what is thy neighbor's right.

Contents cover a preface, the Sabbath controversy, and Barnabas against the Sabbath. Letters to editors of the Advent Harbinger and Bible Advocate follow, with past and present experience. Later sections treat scriptural observance of the Sabbath under the gospel, its beginning, and a last experiment on definite time. Bates argues a Sabbatarian case with scripture and history.
30619-epistle-sermons-vol-3-trinity-sund:
Prof. John Nicholas Lenker translates Luther's Epistle Sermons, volume three, from Trinity Sunday to Advent, with help from others, published in Minneapolis in 1909 by the Luther Press. Lenker, author of Lutherans in All Lands and translator of Luther's works, presents volume nine of Luther's complete works in this third thousand.

A dedication addresses laymen of evangelical Christendom who seek a deeper Christian life from the spiritual classics of Protestant church fathers. These sermons apply pure doctrine to everyday life. A foreword calls the book the English Luther on his twelfth visit to the home, in peasant boots and direct speech. The volume serves pastors and lay readers alike.
30642-aurora-the-magnificent:
Gertrude Hall writes Aurora the Magnificent, copyrighted in 1916 and 1917 and published in March 1917 by the Century Company of New York, illustrated by Gerald Leake. Hall, author of The Truth About Camilla and The Unknown Quantity, dedicates the book to her sister Grace, without whom it would not have been, and to Helen R., without whom it would have been different.

Illustrations show Aurora alone in her room looking at another portrait, standing toward a sanctuary, and clasping her hands in delight like the coo of a dove. A scene has Mrs. Hawthorne asking about sight-seeing plans. Hall writes a society novel of a magnificent heroine, family, and feeling, in polished early twentieth-century prose.
30791-with-joffre-at-verdun-a-story-of-t:
F. S. Brereton, a lieutenant-colonel, wrote this 1916 boys' adventure tale about the Western Front in the First World War, with pictures by Arch. Webb. It belongs to a long run of Brereton war stories, from French at the Front to campaigns in Palestine and Flanders. It sets its hero among French forces at Verdun under General Joffre. The book was made for young readers in wartime Britain.

The story follows its hero through trench fighting, danger, and comradeship at one of the war's hardest sieges, with a sergeant of his platoon wounded in the frontispiece scene. Brereton stresses courage, loyalty, and quick action, in the style of his other service tales. Modern readers will find a vivid but old-fashioned war story, useful as both adventure and a window on how the war was told to boys at home.
3090-complete-original-short-stories-of-:
All thirteen volumes stand together in this complete Maupassant, from Boule de Suif to the last ironies. Volume one opens with Boule de Suif, Two Friends, The Lancer's Wife, The Prisoners, Two Little Soldiers, Father Milon, A Coup d'Etat, Lieutenant Lare's Marriage, and Mademoiselle Fifi. Later volumes run through The Colonel's Ideas, Miss Harriet, and the tales of Normandy, Paris, and war. A mountain passage shows Kunsi tortured at heart over an old man lying on snow, his body never recovered nor laid in consecrated churchyard earth.

By daylight he eats, feeds his dog, and sits motionless, until night brings new terrors and he walks up and down. The complete text lets readers own Maupassant whole, from his first masterpieces to his last ironies.
31108-violence-and-the-labor-movement:
Robert Hunter's 1914 study, reprinted by Macmillan in 1922, examines violence inside the labor movement, and it is dedicated to Eugene V. Debs and to D. Douglas Wilson, the blind and paralyzed trail-blazer for labor. Part one traces terrorism in western Europe, from its father through insurrections, the propaganda of the deed, Johann Most in America, and a series of tragedies, asking what caused them.

Part two follows the struggles with violence: the birth of modern socialism, the battle between Marx and Bakounin, and the fight for existence. It ends with the newest and oldest anarchisms and visions of victory. Hunter writes as a socialist critic of terror, and the book remains a frank early history of a movement arguing with itself.
3113-some-causes-of-the-prevailing-disco:
Warner takes the Declaration of Independence as his text and rewrites its opening sternly. If it had said all men are created unequal, he argues, it would still have stated a truth. If it had added that men are born with duties no society can ignore safely, it would have laid down a needed corollary. Rights without duties leave the argument half made, in his view.

The essay traces current discontent to that missing half. Its politics is a politics of claims, with too little talk of obligation. Duty, Warner insists, is the missing half of every rights claim, and discontent grows where it is left out. Warner meets it with a language of duty, and shows why he thought the omission bred unrest.
31287-turnover-point:
Alfred Coppel's story, printed in Amazing Stories in April-May 1953, follows Pop Ganlon, an old spaceman and father who prospects asteroids. He hauls light freight and occasional passengers through the Belt in his rusting ship, The Luck. Few knew a son of Pop's served in the Patrol, and fewer knew when the boy was killed by a blaster in a Lower Marsport alley. After that Pop kept eating and breathing while his life, in the story's phrase, was over.

In Yakki, down-canal from Marsport, a boneyard spaceport for skippers who cannot pay the big ramp's tariff, John Kane finds Pop and becomes his ticket to a sort of personal immortality. The magazine's headnote frames Pop as one of every era's forgotten men, given a chance to contribute to the society that forgot him. Wistful and hard-bitten, the tale gives an old drifter one last turn at meaning.
3141-the-irish-race-in-the-past-and-the-:
Augustin Thebaud, a Jesuit priest, writes this history of the Irish people past and present. He traces a race shaped by faith, conquest, and exile, from early Christian Ireland through centuries of English rule to the emigrant generations of his own day. The book speaks from within the Catholic tradition it describes.

Thebaud's aim is to give Irish readers a continuous story of their own people, not a set of scattered episodes. Kings, saints, rebels, and emigrants pass in order, with the Church as a steady thread. The volume now serves as a record of how Irish history was told in the nineteenth century, by a writer who loved his subject and did not hide it.
31520-books-condemned-to-be-burnt:
James Anson Farrer's Books Condemned to be Burnt, published in London by Elliot Stock in 1892 and edited for the Book-Lover's Library by Henry B. Wheatley, traces book-burning in England from its first instance by the common hangman to its last. Farrer's preface calls this the kind of question a rational curiosity asks. Yet it is often hardest to answer, since historians dwell on battles, all drearily similar, rather than on such matters.

Chapters follow book-fires through the centuries, beginning with sixteenth-century burnings. Farrer treats censorship as history, tracing which books offended church and state and why. Readers of book history will find a learned, entertaining study of suppression. Its subject remains timely: the public burning of a book says as much about the burners as about the book.
31612-the-very-secret-agent:
Mari Wolf's science-fiction story The Very Secret Agent, dated 1954, opens in a ship just beyond the orbit of Mars. There two aliens, Riuku and Nagor, look at each other. Riuku has had no luck, and he tells Nagor that no one else will either, since the Earthmen are too well shielded. He contacted the factory easily enough. The parking lot attendant knows a new weapon is being produced there, and so does the waitress across the street at the Jumbo Burger Grill. No one knows anything about what it is.

The headnote jokes that poor Riuku, being no human, can hardly be expected to grasp how a woman thinks. The male of the same species does not even know.
31627-volcanoes-past-and-present:
Edward Hull's Volcanoes, Past and Present, in the Contemporary Science Series edited by Havelock Ellis, was published at London by Walter Scott in 1892. Hull was examiner in geology to the University of London, and his book carries forty-one illustrations and four plates of rock sections, in six parts. Its first figure shows the eruption of Vesuvius in 1872 and 1873.

The book treats volcanoes as they were and as they are, joining the record of past eruptions to the geology of the present day. Hull writes for general readers of science, and he uses pictures and rock sections to show what words alone cannot carry.
3168-poems-of-the-past-and-the-present:
Thomas Hardy published Poems of the Past and the Present in 1901, dated 1902, as his second book of verse after Wessex Poems. This 1919 Macmillan edition reprints it with the same care as its companion volume. The poems look back at a century ending and a new one beginning, with war, parting, and the ironies of progress among their themes.

The Darkling Thrush, Hardy's most famous lyric, belongs to this book, singing hope from a bare winter landscape at the turn of the year. Other poems weigh the Boer War dead, lost loves, and the gap between promise and fact. Readers who know Hardy's novels will hear the same grave music here, compressed into lines that refuse easy comfort.
3179-the-american-claimant:
Mark Twain published this novel in 1892 around a disputed English title. The Earl of Rossmore faces the American claimant, and Viscount Berkeley proposes to change places with him. Berkeley then decides to visit America, while Colonel Mulberry Sellers tends his art gallery and receives Washington Hawkins. Hawkins brings news that he is the congressional delegate from the Cherokee Strip.

The comedy grows from swapped rank and American optimism meeting English form. Sellers, Twain's great dreamer of fortunes, anchors the farce. The novel is lighter than Twain's best work, but its satire still bites: titles, claims, and inventions all promise wealth, and all keep their promise just out of reach.
31806-the-house-of-fulfilment:
George Madden Martin's 1904 novel The House of Fulfilment was published by McClure, Phillips and Company. It opens with seventeen-year-old Harriet Blair traveling with her father, mother, and brother Austen to New Orleans for the marriage of her older brother Alexander. The Blairs decline the bride's family's hospitality and attend punctiliously from their hotel.

Alexander Blair the father, a banker and capitalist of Vermont stock and now the richest man in Louisville, is stern and rugged, while his wife brings thrifty closeness and strong practical sense. Readers get a novel of American family life and ambition, following Harriet from girlhood toward the fulfillment of its title.
3181-the-stolen-white-elephant:
Mark Twain left this tale out of A Tramp Abroad, fearing some particulars looked exaggerated and others untrue. Before those doubts proved groundless, the book had gone to press. The story itself comes from a chance railway acquaintance, a gentleman past seventy whose good, gentle face and earnest manner stamped his words as sincere.

What follows is a detective farce: a sacred white elephant, bound for a royal gift, vanishes in transit, and a swarm of detectives takes the trail. Twain mocks official method at every turn, as clues multiply and the elephant stays lost. The tale is short, brisk, and pure Twain: a solemn inquiry collapsing under its own machinery.
31819-ku-klux-klan-its-origin-growth-and:
J. C. Lester and D. L. Wilson's history of the Ku Klux Klan, with an introduction by Walter L. Fleming, professor of history at West Virginia University, traces the secret order from its origin through its spread, transformation, decline, and disbandment. Its five chapters are illustrated with photographs of badges, costumes, meeting rooms, and leaders including General Nathan Bedford Forrest.

Four appendices print the Klan's prescripts, the constitution of a local order, and its orders, warnings, and oaths. Readers get an early historical study of Reconstruction's most notorious secret society, valuable as a source on its organization and rituals, and written from a standpoint modern readers will read critically.
31876-the-christian-view-of-the-old-test:
Frederick Carl Eiselen's Christian View of the Old Testament, published by the Methodist Book Concern with copyright in 1912, argues for the Old Testament's place in Christian thought and life. Eiselen, a professor at Garrett Biblical Institute, observes that up to the mid-second century, the Old Testament alone counted as authoritative scripture.

Chapters cover the New Testament view of the Old Testament, the Old Testament and modern science, modern criticism, and archaeology. Readers get a thoughtful early twentieth-century introduction, written for students and ministers, that takes both faith and scholarship seriously. It speaks to readers who want faith and hard study in one book.
32044-jimmy-kirkland-and-the-plot-for-a-:
Hugh S. Fullerton's 1915 novel Jimmy Kirkland and the Plot for a Pennant, illustrated by Charles Paxson Gray and published in Philadelphia by the John C. Winston Company, is dedicated to Charles A. Comiskey, the man to whom, more than all others, the honesty and high standard of professional baseball is due. Its thirty-two chapters run from Panthers or Bears through a miracle called McCarthy, the tempter, Adonis makes a deal. McCarthy in disgrace to a race to save the day and the plotters foiled.

The first chapter opens with the loss in the final series' opening game between the Panthers and Bears, a hard blow to the Bears' championship hopes. Readers get a boys' baseball novel of gambling plots, kidnapping, and fair play.
32104-turning-point:
Alfred Coppel's short story, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in November 1953, turns on a director's impossible choice. Its tagline frames it as a choice between lesser evils. Merrick must choose between saving people and saving humanity itself. The story's world makes that choice concrete.

An epigraph from Quintus Bland's Romance of Genus Homo describes the Creche in the year 2500. It is a huge blind cube on a ragged mountain, above bare slopes falling to a turbulent sea. For five centuries the Creche has stood so, and androids have come forth in an unending stream to labour for Man, the Master. Director Han Merrick, thin and pale, warns Virginia that prying can only precipitate a pogrom, with Erikson a bigot of the worst kind.
3235-a-first-year-in-canterbury-settleme:
Samuel Butler writes this account of his first year in the Canterbury settlement of New Zealand. The book, sixth in a series of his works, records a young Englishman's passage to a new colony and his first seasons of colonial work. Sheep, land, weather, and neighbors fill the narrative, with the practical detail of a man learning a country from scratch.

Butler later turned the same experience into fiction, but here it stands as fact. The value lies in its plainness: prices, problems, and small triumphs, set down without romance. Readers interested in emigration get a firsthand report of what a first year abroad really cost, in money, labor, and loneliness, and what it returned.
32397-visits-to-monasteries-in-the-levan:
Robert Curzon's travel book, published in London in 1849, recounts visits to monasteries in the Levant, drawn from time spent among old manuscripts in a family country house. Curzon, the Honourable Robert Curzon junior, travelled in the East when books about palm trees, camels, and pyramids already filled the shelves. His excuse for one more volume is the monasteries themselves, their libraries, and their daily rule.

An opening plate shows the great monastery of Meteora, seen from Barlaam across the river Peneus. Another shows a monk calling monks to prayer by beating a wooden board, the simandro, used in place of bells. The book mixes travel, history, and manuscript hunting, giving readers a first-hand look at Greek monastic life in the mid-nineteenth century.
32399-reminiscences-the-story-of-an-emig:
Hans Mattson's memoir, published in Saint Paul in 1891, tells the story of a Swedish emigrant who later served as United States consul general in India. Mattson begins with ancestry, a country home in Sweden, early school years, Christmas customs, and military life, before his departure for America. His first chapters then follow arrival at Boston, travel to New York and Buffalo, and farm work in New Hampshire.

Later he journeys to Illinois, works on a railroad, suffers the ague, and meets Doctor Ober, among other early American trials. The memoir reads as a plain, detailed account of starting over in a new country: work, sickness, faith, and family ties. It gives readers a migrant's view of nineteenth-century America from Sweden to the Midwest.
32570-zeppelin-the-story-of-a-great-achi:
Harry Vissering's Zeppelin, published in Chicago in August 1922, honours Count Zeppelin, 1838 to 1917, for vision and unfaltering devotion that gave the rigid airship to the world. Vissering quotes Zeppelin at Friedrichshafen in May 1914: forces of nature cannot be eliminated, but they may be balanced against each other. An epigraph from Horace Mann compares a savage swimming a river with a dozen pounds to modern steel leviathans bearing millionfold burdens across the earth.

Illustrations show Count Zeppelin and Dr. Ludwig Dürr, chief engineer associated with Zeppelin from the start, with the German Airship Transportation Company, DELAG, carrying passengers in its early years. Vissering traces trials, crashes, and triumphs that turned a daring idea into scheduled air travel. The book remains a vivid, admiring history of the airship age.
3265-the-re-creation-of-brian-kent:
Harold Bell Wright frames this novel as a letter to Auntie Sue. He wonders, while writing his simple story of life and love, whether she will forgive him for putting her in a book. He imagines her protest: she never did the things he makes her do, and never lived the life he gives her. The joke carries a serious point about fiction's debts to real people.

Brian Kent himself is the man remade by the title's promise. Wright, beloved for The Shepherd of the Hills, writes of second chances in plain, sentimental prose. A broken life, a new place, and love doing slow rebuilding work: Wright's recipe for a second chance.
32709-shock-treatment:
Stanley Mullen sets this tale in Venusport, where Spud Newlin tends bar at the Spacebell. It is payday night, among sportsmen, widows, and pink elephants. A strange young woman enters, sad and out of place in her drab, expensive dress. Her luminous eyes are full of fear, and Newlin feels a powerful impulse to protect her.

The woman, Songeen, offers a cure for the sickness of life itself. Her husband and the Protection Police drive the pair out of the city, with mechanical hounds on their trail. In the Venusian wastelands and a dreamlike forest of shifting shapes, Newlin learns what her cure costs. He learns too what it means to follow her.
32719-mr-president:
Stephen Arr tells of George Wong, overwhelmingly elected President of the Solar Union. His story appeared in Galaxy Science Fiction in November 1953. Returns from Venus alone give Wong nearly three and a half billion votes. His rivals Thompson, Miccio, and Kau trail far behind, with twenty-five vice-presidents still to settle.

Wong organized the colonization of Io and Europa, and he holds a Responsibility Quotient of 9.6. Yet he greets victory with dread rather than joy. Drafted by the conventions, he faces a ceremonial duty that chills him. He must present a citation to the shattered remains of the Third Company. They are veterans of a policing mission in the Veganea system, whose scarred faces confront their new president.
32939-the-sacred-fount:
Henry James's 1901 novel The Sacred Fount follows a narrator who arrives at a large country-house party and begins to watch its guests with growing suspicion. At the station he already scans fellow travelers for friends and possible enemies, and on meeting Gilbert Long he senses an element worth watching. The party that follows becomes, in his mind, a puzzle of looks, talk, and shifting pairs.

James builds the novel almost entirely from that watching: who is lively and who is drained, and who has gained wit at whose expense. The question is whether a sacred fount of youth and talk can be traced from one guest to another. The narrator's theory may be brilliance or self-deception, and James leaves the reader to judge. It is a subtle, talk-driven novel about perception itself, and one of James's most argued experiments in point of view.
32951-the-bull-run-rout-scenes-attending:
Edward Henry Clement's Bull-Run Rout preserves a short paper written years earlier by his late brother. It was printed from the proceedings of the Massachusetts Historical Society for March 1909. His brother watched the rout at Bull Run with a boy's eyes and a boy's love of the marvelous. Clement values it for the battle scene and for its picture of the public mind on the eve of the great uprising. Northerners still believed the war cloud might pass.

The paper argues that the Civil War, as a war, was a surprise to the North. It adds that up to the day of Bull Run most people hoped fighting would be avoided. It is a brief, vivid memoir, useful to historians for its feeling as much as its facts. It also speaks to general readers through its boy's-eye view of a nation's rude awakening.
33072-stevenson-s-perfect-virtues-as-exe:
Luther A. Brewer's Stevenson's Perfect Virtues, privately printed at Cedar Rapids at Christmas 1922 for friends, takes its text from Robert Louis Stevenson: gentleness and cheerfulness are the perfect virtues. Brewer argues that Stevenson was right, that cheerfulness is among the most admirable traits of character, and that joined with gentleness it makes a companionable and beloved man. Both virtues, he says, were held in emphatic measure by Stevenson and by Leigh Hunt.

The short book therefore pairs the two writers, explaining why Hunt grows in esteem as lovers and students of early nineteenth-century English literature come to know him better. It is a personal tribute rather than a formal study, written for friends who shared Brewer's admiration. Readers who enjoy Stevenson and Hunt will find it a warm, brief meditation on the qualities that make a writer good company.
33207-the-perfume-of-eros-a-fifth-avenue:
Edgar Saltus's Perfume of Eros, a Fifth Avenue incident published in New York in 1905, follows fashionable New York. Its chapters cover a man of fashion, a pocket Venus, an ex-first lady, enchantment, Marie changing her name, and the yellow fay. They go on to sweet-and-twenty, two in a turret, and Fanny changing her clothes, before a victim and general sessions. Saltus writes the city as a stage for desire and artifice.

The novel's title points to love as scent, alluring, brief, and hard to hold, and its Fifth Avenue setting gives Saltus room for satire on wealth, beauty, and manners. His prose is polished and decadent, fond of epigram and of the irony that follows a fashionable fall. The book remains a sharp, short novel of New York society at its most gilded, for readers who enjoy Saltus's elegant disenchantment.
33222-the-irish-at-the-front:
Michael MacDonagh's book follows Irish regiments at the front in the First World War, from the retreat from Mons to the great push at Loos. Its chapters tell how the Munsters saved their guns, how the Irish Guards rallied at the Marne, and how the Dublins and Munsters landed at the Dardanelles. MacDonagh, author of Irish Life and Character, draws on the accounts of the men themselves.

The volume moves battle by battle, honoring regiments and their war honors while keeping the focus on soldiers in the line. Gas, liquid fire, rest camps, and Victoria Cross deeds all find a place in its plain, stirring narrative. For readers of Irish and military history, it is a vivid record of Ireland's part in the war, told with pride and care.
3326-the-well-beloved-a-sketch-of-a-temp:
Thomas Hardy calls this book a sketch of a temperament, and its ground is Portland stone. A peninsula carved by Time out of a single stone holds most of the scenes. It has been home for centuries to a curious and nearly distinct people, with strange beliefs and singular customs now mostly obsolescent. Fancies there, Hardy says, thrive by the sea as soft plants thrive where inland frosts cannot reach.

The temperament belongs to Jocelyn Pierston, a sculptor chasing his ideal, the well-beloved, through three generations of one family. Each Avice seems to hold the vision, and each slips away. The novel is Hardy's lightest in manner and saddest in moral: an artist's ideal, pursued faithfully, proves the one love that never stays.
33350-the-arts-and-crafts-movement:
T. J. Cobden-Sanderson's essay on the Arts and Crafts Movement, printed in 1905 by the Hammersmith Publishing Society, defines a movement that sought to bring human work under the influence of art. Cobden-Sanderson sees the movement as part of a wider shift in ideas at the close of the last century. It was an effort to make craft, not mere machine work, the supreme mode of human activity.

The essay is short and thoughtful, aimed at readers who care about making, beauty, and honest work. Its argument still speaks to debates about craft and industry, hand and machine. For students of design history, it is a founding statement, written by a man who lived the movement he describes, in plain, earnest prose.
33386-the-tremendous-event:
Maurice Le Blanc's Tremendous Event, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and copyrighted in 1922, opens with an author's note. The note concerns the tremendous event itself. Le Blanc, famed for Arsène Lupin, here turns to a tale of mystery and wonder. Isabel is asked whether she regrets anything, a whisper that hints at love and loss behind the plot. The novel's scenes move between intimate talk and vast, strange happenings.

The book blends romance with speculative wonder, as Le Blanc's imagination leaps from drawing rooms to events that shake the world. Its pace is brisk, its mood both tender and thrilling. For readers who enjoy Le Blanc beyond Lupin, The Tremendous Event offers a bold, unusual novel, full of surprise and feeling.
33924-marion-darche-a-story-without-comm:
F. Marion Crawford wrote this New York novel, published in 1893 by Macmillan. Marion Darche opens with a striking image: New York society as a map of fitted pieces, each of a different shape, size, and color, yet forming a compact whole. Crawford argues that New York lacks the fixed scale of London or Paris society.

The story that follows moves through that social map without authorial comment, as its title promises. Readers watch rank, talk, and manners sort themselves out. The novel offers a cool, observant portrait of New York life in the 1890s.
3427-kilo-being-the-love-story-of-eliph-:
Ellis Parker Butler tells a comic love story about Eliph Hewlitt, a traveling book agent in a small American town. Eliph knows horses as well as he knows human nature, and his courtship of Susan runs through chapters with titles such as How to Win the Affections and Second: A Small Present. A horse named Kilo, a castaway, a colonel, and a boss grafter all tangle the plot.

Butler's humor lies in small town schemes, false gods, and the gap between sales talk and real feeling. Eliph sells books for a living, yet he must learn a harder lesson about winning a heart. Readers who enjoy gentle American comedy will find a light romance, full of local color and sly jokes about agents and their pitches.
4314-appendicitis-the-etiology-hygenic-a:
John H. Tilden, a physician, wrote this book on appendicitis from a drugless, hygienic standpoint. He treats the causes of the disease first, then its dietetic and hygienic care, arguing that faulty habits of eating and living prepare the ground for attacks. His aim is prevention and natural recovery rather than routine surgery.

Tilden's chapters set out his theory of disease as the result of enervation and toxic buildup, applied here to one organ. Modern readers should note that his advice reflects early twentieth-century alternative medicine, not current practice. The book remains a document of that movement, and of the debate over surgery for appendicitis.
4905-galusha-the-magnificent:
Joseph C. Lincoln's Galusha the Magnificent opens on a foggy October afternoon, as Horatio Pulcifer walks home between Wellmouth Centre and East Wellmouth through rain, puddles, and pitch-pine groves. The Cape Cod setting, wet and gray, frames a comedy of village life in which an unlikely hero earns his grand title.

Lincoln's humor rests on local character: plainspoken neighbors, small-town pride, and the gap between a man's reputation and his actual deeds. The novel moves at a village pace, with weather and gossip doing much of the work. Readers get a gentle, funny portrait of Cape life, told by a writer who knew its people from the inside.
5669-considerations-on-representative-go:
John Stuart Mill's treatise asks which form of government best serves a people, and answers that representative government, rightly built, fits a society ready to use it. Mill opens by treating forms of government as a matter of choice, not fate. He then sets a test for any good government. It must manage public business well, and it must improve the character of its citizens. Later chapters weigh the dangers of majority rule, the reach of the vote, and how voting should work.

The book stays practical even when it turns philosophical, since Mill keeps asking what institutions actually do to ordinary people. He defends broad participation while warning that unchecked majorities can crush minorities, and he treats education and open debate as guards against that harm. Modern readers will find here the classic case for elected rule, with its hopes and its cautions stated in full.
5736-the-professional-aunt:
Mary Wemyss opens The Professional Aunt with a wry observation. Parents often choose a boy's profession for him. So the shrewd, business-like child may become a painter, while the artistic, unpractical one joins the Stock Exchange. The novel that follows turns that irony on family life, as an aunt takes up her calling with professional seriousness. Chapters follow households, children, and the adults who try to manage them.

Readers get light, observant comedy about English family life, where aunts, nephews, and nieces negotiate affection and duty. Wemyss writes with humor and warmth, letting character do the work of plot. The book suits readers who enjoy domestic novels of manners, and anyone who has known a relative whose real profession was holding a family together.
5900-umboo-the-elephant:
Howard Garis introduces Baby Umboo, a young elephant, in a circus cage on a sweltering day. Chako, one of the monkeys, cries that it is too hot for anything. It is hotter under the tent than ever it was in the jungle. He hangs by his tail, swinging from a wooden bar. In the jungle, Chako recalls, they could find a pool of water, a comfort the tent denies.

Young readers follow Umboo through circus life and jungle memory, with animal friends who talk, tease, and help. Garis writes in short, friendly chapters suited to bedtime, favoring gentle adventure over fright. The book suits early readers who love elephants, and families who enjoy animal tales where a baby hero learns the world one hot afternoon at a time.
6435-the-principles-of-scientific-manage:
Frederick Winslow Taylor, in 1911, sets management's principal object as maximum prosperity for employer and for each employee together. Maximum prosperity means more than large dividends: it means every branch developed to highest excellence so prosperity lasts. For employees it means more than higher wages: it means each man developed to maximum efficiency, fitted to the highest grade of work his abilities allow, and given that work when possible.

President Roosevelt, Taylor recalls, called conservation of national resources only preliminary to the larger question of national efficiency. Taylor came to Midvale Steel's machine shop in 1878, after apprenticeship as pattern maker and machinist, in depression after the panic of 1873, when mechanics could hardly find trade work. His book argues that science, not rule of thumb, must govern the shop, for both sides' good.
6464-shop-management:
Frederick Winslow Taylor's Shop Management, dated 1911, grows from years of changing shop methods in manufacturing and industrial establishments across many trades. Two facts strike him most. First, the great unevenness, even in best run works, in the development of management's several elements. Second, the lack of apparent relation between good shop management and the payment of dividends. Trusts may dominate the day, yet each component company was built largely through individual energies.

A mid passage warns that piece work, where price alone is specified without limiting time, can let output fall off largely without management noticing. Hence Taylor's first of four principles for the best type of management: a large daily task for each man, with adequate measures taken alongside. The book is a manager's field report, practical and insistent on system over habit.
659-paul-the-peddler-or-the-fortunes-of-:
Horatio Alger, Jr. writes a boys' tale of New York street life in this volume. Paul, a young peddler, works the streets among bootblacks, newsboys, and shopkeepers, learning honesty, thrift, and pluck. A biography fronts the book, tracing Alger from Revere birth and Harvard to a pastorate and then to writing for street boys.

Alger writes with plain, earnest prose, full of city scenes and moral lessons. His heroes rise by work and character, not luck alone. The book endures as a typical Alger story, where a street merchant's fortunes turn on industry and a clean heart.
6617-poems-of-sentiment:
Wilcox returns in Poems of Sentiment, a 1919 London reprint of a book first issued in 1909 and reprinted many times. Double Carnations, Never Mind, Two Women, and It All Will Come Out Right open a set that runs through love, time, will, regret, and Easter morn. A little white hearse and a yellow-covered almanac add a somber, homely note.

The verse is direct and musical, with feeling worn openly and morals drawn in plain words. Wilcox does not hide behind hard images; she speaks to the heart at once. Poems of Sentiment suits readers who want verse that comforts, cheers, and names what love and loss feel like.
6762-politics-a-treatise-on-government:
Aristotle's Politics, in William Ellis's translation, is the second part of a treatise whose first part is the Ethics. The introduction notes that Aristotle did not split statesman from moralist as modern readers tend to do. Ethics paints the character needed for a good life, lived in society, and its last chapters turn to the statesman's legislative work.

Politics itself asks what makes a city just, stable, and good, weighing constitutions, citizens, and laws. Ellis's Dent edition, first issued in 1912, keeps the prose clear and scholarly. Politics is a founding work of political thought, still argued over by readers today.
6764-army-life-in-a-black-regiment:
Thomas Wentworth Higginson records the First South Carolina Volunteers, the first slave regiment mustered into United States service in the Civil War. First published in 1869 and reprinted in 1900, the book runs from a camp diary up the St. Mary's, St. John's, and Edisto rivers to picket duty, a night in the water, and life at Camp Shaw. Negro spirituals get a chapter of their own.

Higginson, their white colonel, writes with respect for his Black soldiers, their courage, humor, and faith. An appendix lists officers, first Black soldiers, and the struggle for equal pay. Army Life in a Black Regiment is a classic, first-hand Civil War memoir, essential to American history.
7033-picturesque-quebec-a-sequel-to-queb:
J M Lemoine offers Picturesque Quebec as a sequel to his Quebec Past and Present of 1876, inscribed to the citizens of Quebec. The preface promises to complete the city's history with new details on the spot where Samuel de Champlain settled in 1608. A rapid glance covers incidents, sights, objects, edifices, city gates, and improvements ancient and modern, as an antiquarian's ramble round streets, squares, and promenades may disclose.

Lemoine hopes the book will serve as a copious store of historical, topographical, legendary, industrial, and antiquarian lore, gathered not without trouble. Monuments, public and private buildings, and old walls all find a place. The volume is a loving guide to a city proud of its French roots and its stone walls.
7090-the-little-immigrant:
The Little Immigrant, privately printed in 1921 and surviving in few copies, tells how the author's great grandmother's parents met, married, and began a family. The introduction, by a great grandson, explains most names are disguised, though thinly, and gives a table matching false names to real ones. Renestine Jewel stands for Ernestine Jacobowsky, Aldine Bilter for her married sister, and Jaffray Starr for Jacob Sterne.

Lola, Ena, Lester, Andrew, and Frank stand for Laura, Eva, Leopold, Alfred, and Fred Sterne, while Josiah the longtime family slave and his wife appear with their counterparts. General Buell, whom the Starrs housed during Reconstruction after Civil War violence, keeps his true name. The book is a family memoir of immigration, marriage, and the postwar South.
7168-introduction-to-the-old-testament:
John Edgar McFadyen wrote this introduction for students, ministers, and lay readers who want the modern view of the Old Testament as a whole. He warns at once that he offers nothing for specialists, since the details of full study are intricate, perplexing, and all but countless. His aim is the wood rather than the trees.

The book therefore maps the shape of the whole testament before it dwells on single parts, helping a busy reader grasp how scholars now read these old books. McFadyen, a professor at Knox College in Toronto, keeps his prose clear and direct, so that a reader without time for deep research can still follow the main lines of the argument.
7262-the-country-housewife-and-lady-s-di:
R. Bradley's Country Housewife and Lady's Director teaches the management of a house and the delights and profits of a farm, month by month from the year's beginning to its end. Its instructions cover the brew-house and malt liquors in the cellar, wines of all sorts, and the dairy. Butter and cheese on the worst of soils, brawn, fish, fowl, herbs, and roots follow, in the most elegant manner for the table.

Distilling, ketchup, and many curious and durable sauces join practical observations on ordering a country seat. Bradley writes for a housewife who must be steward, cook, and farmer at once, and his tone is plain and thrifty. The book turns household work into a yearly craft, useful and, in its own way, elegant.
7370-second-treatise-of-government:
John Locke's Second Treatise, published in 1689, is one of the founding texts of liberal political thought. Locke wrote against the claim that kings rule by divine right, answering Sir Robert Filmer's defense of absolute monarchy. In its place he sets out a theory of government built on the consent of the governed, written while England was settling its own revolution against a king.

Locke argues that people are naturally free and equal, holding rights to life, liberty, and property before any government exists. Rulers hold power only as a trust, to protect those rights, and a government that turns tyrannical may be resisted. The argument later shaped the American and French revolutions, and it still frames debates about rights, consent, and the limits of state power.
7428-the-consumer-viewpoint:
Mildred Maddocks directed the Good Housekeeping Institute's department of household engineering, and this book reports what that department learned from years of testing household devices. It covers vital phases of manufacturing and selling. How is a device designed? How will it actually be used in a home? How can the maker guard against misuse it never foresaw?

The viewpoint of the title is the buyer's. Maddocks argues that designers and factory managers must think past known conditions of use to the care and skill real households bring. The book speaks to manufacturers and dealers, but its lessons still read clearly: test things as people will use them, not as engineers wish they would. It is an early classic of consumer research.
7549-quotes-and-images-from-the-short-st:
Guy de Maupassant's short stories fill thirteen volumes and number some 180 tales. They are the foundation of the modern short story, and this volume gathers quotations and images from them. The first volume alone contains Boule de Suif, Two Friends, The Lancer's Wife, The Prisoners, Father Milon, and Mademoiselle Fifi, with a study by Pol Neveux.

Later volumes add The Colonel's Ideas, Mother Sauvage, Madame Baptiste, and The Blind Man. They add the famous Piece of String, with The Model, My Uncle Jules, The Orphan, The Beggar, and The Parrot among the contents. Maupassant's world is Norman peasants, Paris clerks, soldiers, and lovers, all caught in a twist of fate. The quotation volume is a map to that world, story by story.
7560-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-c:
Anthony Hamilton's Memoirs of Count Grammont paints the court of Charles II, and this companion volume gathers short passages and pictures from it. Notes by Sir Walter Scott frame the memoirs for later readers. Grammont, a witty exile at the Restoration court, stands at the center of the scenes. Each passage can be traced back to its full scene, so a striking line never has to stand alone.

Read together, the passages sketch a court ruled by wit, memory, and manners. Ambition, grudges, flattery, and the art of holding favor recur across them, often in a single sharp turn. The pictures add faces and dress to the talk. It works as a short cut into a famous memoir: lively, gossipy, and sharp about how people rose or fell by what they said.
7782-the-last-tournament:
Alfred Tennyson's The Last Tournament, in the author's edition, sits between Pelleas and Guinevere in the Idylls of the King. It opens with Dagonet the fool, made mock-knight by Gawain, dancing like a withered leaf before the hall at Camelot, high above yellowing woods.

Tristram enters with harp in hand and a ruby carcanet, prize of yesterday's jousts, and asks why the fool skips so. Behind the jest lies a darker tale: Arthur and Lancelot once rescued a babe from an eagle's nest, and gave her to a queen who took her coldly. The poem marks Camelot's late decline.
8081-louisa-pallant:
Henry James set this short novel at Homburg, opening on the terrace of the Kursaal on a beautiful night toward the end of July. The narrator, waiting for his young nephew, meets Louisa Pallant, a woman he thought he knew completely, and receives a revelation about her character that startles and touches him. The story that follows revisits old acquaintance, a mother's hopes, and a young man's summer in Europe.

James's interest is in what people hide, even from friends of years, and how one confession can recast a whole past. The tale is brief and elegantly told, with the spa town as its stage. It is a fine small example of James's art of nuance, and a good starting point for readers new to his shorter fiction.
8095-awful-disclosures-of-the-hotel-dieu:
Maria Monk's Awful Disclosures, with a continuation of her narrative after her escape from the Hotel Dieu nunnery of Montreal, became one of the best-selling books of the nineteenth century. Monk claimed to expose secret crimes inside the convent, and her story fed fierce anti-Catholic feeling in America. A transcriber's note warns that some page scans were illegible, and that chapter fourteen was missing from both contents and book, presumably a printing error.

The book's claims were widely disputed at the time and later discredited, yet it remains historically important as propaganda. It shows how a sensational tale could move public opinion and sell by the hundred thousand. Readers should approach it as a document of prejudice and popular print, not as reliable history of convent life.
8150-a-street-of-paris-and-its-inhabitan:
Honoré de Balzac wrote this little Parisian silhouette in prose to open a new series of the Comédie Humaine, while the first series was still finishing. Translated by Henri Pene du Bois and illustrated by François Courboin, it appeared in a limited New York edition of 1900, with four hundred copies printed.
