From his porch he looks out on fields and a curving town road, glad for the human cord that binds him to them all. The book praises slow travel and plain neighbors.
the-harris-ingram-experiment: Charles E. Bolton, M.A., wrote The Harris-Ingram Experiment, published in Cleveland by The Burrows Brothers Company in 1905. Bolton is named as the author of A Model Village and Other Papers and Travels in Europe and America, and the book is dedicated to his wife and son. Contents chapters include The Harrises in New York, Mr. Hugh Searles of London Arrives, A Bad Send-off, and Aboard the S.S. Majestic. Nothing past the front matter is present here.
the-high-deeds-of-finn-and-other-bardic-: T. W. Rolleston wrote The High Deeds of Finn and Other Bardic Romances of Ancient Ireland, with an introduction by Stopford A. Brooke and sixteen pictures by Stephen Reid, published in New York by Thomas Y. Crowell & Company. A note explains that one Finn tale, The Pursuit of Dermot and Grania, was left out in part because it shows Finn in a light at odds with the rest. The contents begin with The Story of the Children of Lir. Only the title page, note, and contents are present here.
the-irish-race-in-the-past-and-the-prese: The Reverend Aug. J. Thebaud, S.J., wrote this history of the Irish race. The pages present here hold only an old etext header. Nothing of the book itself appears. The header names the title and the author. License and donation boilerplate fills the rest. The text dates from around December 2000. No chapter, preface, or page of Thebaud's account can be read here. The record carries the wrapper and not the work. Ireland's past and present stay behind that wrapper.
the-king-s-achievement: Robert Hugh Benson signed this novel's acknowledgments at Cambridge on July 14, 1905. He thanked Dom Bede Camm and Mgr. Barnes for revising proofs, E. Conybeare for the cover's coins, and Abbot Gasquet for books and answers. Benson had written By What Authority before it. Only the preface matter and first contents are present here. The narrative itself does not appear. Book I, The King's Will, moves through a decision, the arrival at Lewes, Master More, and a merry prisoner. It is a Henrician story told from the Catholic side.
the-last-tournament:
Alfred Tennyson places his Arthurian poem between Pelleas and Guinevere among the Idylls of the King. Dagonet, the fool made mock knight by Gawain, dances before the hall at Camelot like a withered leaf. Tristram approaches with a harp and a swaying ruby necklace won in the jousts.

Tennyson then recalls how Arthur and Lancelot once found a crying babe in an eagle nest on a crag. The Queen raised the child, named Nestling, and loved her until early death. The ruby prize from that rescue now hangs over a court already touched by decay.
the-little-immigrant:
Eva Stern wrote The Little Immigrant in 1921, drawing on how her parents met, married, and began a family; the book was privately printed, and few copies survive. An introduction by her great-grandson explains that most names are thinly disguised. Her mother Ernestine, renamed Renestine in the story, is the little immigrant of the title, while General Buell appears under his real name from the Reconstruction years.

Chapter one shows thirteen-year-old Renestine packing her trunk at midnight, dreaming while her mother hurries her along. She is to sail to America to join a married sister already there. Readers get a family story of immigration told from inside, with a key that matches the invented names to the real people behind them.
the-living-present: Gertrude Atherton's The Living Present was published by Frederick A. Stokes Company and dedicated to Eternal France. Only the title page, frontispiece, and part of the contents are present here, so the text does not appear. The contents announce Book I, French Women in War Time. Its chapters include Madame Balli and the "Comfort Package," The Silent Army, and The Munition Makers. Others follow on Mademoiselle Javal and the Éclopés, Madame Pierre Goujon, Valentine Thompson, Madame Waddington, and the Countess d'Haussonville. The list closes with The Woman's Opportunity.
the-log-of-a-noncombatant:
Horace Green, staff correspondent of the New York Evening Post and special correspondent of the Boston Journal, wrote The Log of a Noncombatant in 1915. Chapter one finds him in the Post city room when war broke out in August 1914. A copy boy hands him a telegram from a Boston friend, Willard B. Luther, asking cryptically, "How about this fight?"

The contents map where that question took him: from Broadway to Ghent, the bombardment of Termonde, capture, the bombardment and surrender of Antwerp, and spying on spies. An appendix is titled Atrocities. Green writes as a civilian reporter caught inside a war zone, and his log mixes personal anecdote with front-line observation of Belgium's ordeal.
the-lost-continent:
Edgar Rice Burroughs wrote The Lost Continent, first published under the title Beyond Thirty. Its narrator admits a lifelong fascination with the last days of twentieth-century Europe. Two centuries have passed since contact between the Western and Eastern Hemispheres ceased after the Great War, and censored histories leave Europe's fate a matter of speculation.

He recounts how news still filtered west for fifteen years, until a slogan, "The East for the East, the West for the West," ended all intercourse by statute. Mine-strewn oceans had already killed transoceanic commerce. The last submarine sighted, he says, was the huge Q 138, which attacked a Brazilian tanker near the Bermudas with twenty-nine torpedoes in the fall of 1972. A companion record shares this title but holds a different author's Atlantis novel.
the-man-and-the-moment: Elinor Glyn's The Man and the Moment was published by D. Appleton and Company in 1914, illustrated by R. F. James. Only the title pages and list of illustrations are present, so the novel does not appear. The captions give the flavor. A frontispiece is captioned "It all looked intimate and lover-like." One plate shows a hero bounding forward to meet a heroine. Another shows a table near theirs in a restaurant. A line of dialogue worries that someone is in some scrape and that something must have culminated tonight.
the-moving-picture-boys-on-the-war-front:
Victor Appleton's The Moving Picture Boys on the War Front, subtitled The Hunt for the Stolen Army Films, was published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap with copyright in 1918. Only title page and the start of a contents list are present here, so the story does not appear. A frontispiece caption says it took all three lads' nerve to stand at their posts while men were killed around them.

Contents shown run only to Chapter VI, with page numbers. A Call to Battle starts at page 1, The Accident at page 11, and Monsieur Secor at page 20. All Aboard, Anxious Days, and A Queer Conference follow. Appleton is billed as author of the Tom Swift books on the title page.
the-muse-of-the-department:
Honore de Balzac's The Muse of the Department, translated by James Waring, opens with a dedication letter to the Count Ferdinand de Gramont. Balzac thanks Gramont for devising the coats of arms and mottoes of the great families in his Human Comedy. He calls the resulting armorial, or book of heraldry, a complete manual of French heraldry. He also calls it a monument of friendship and patience.

The novel then begins at Sancerre, a town crowning hills above the Loire on the edge of Le Berry. The river floods the flats below, leaving fertile yellow alluvium, the rich soil rivers deposit, except where a terrible rising has buried fields in sand forever. The little river-port of Saint-Thibault draws its life from the Loire at the hill's foot.
the-new-york-subway-its-construction-and:
The New York Subway: Its Construction and Equipment was issued by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company in New York, with copyright in 1904, and planned and executed by the McGraw Publishing Company. Only a title page and the start of a table of contents are present here, so the engineering chapters do not appear. Illustrations of the power house operating room and the company symbol head the pages.

Contents shown give page numbers for an introduction at page 13 and five chapters. The Route of the Road, covering passenger stations and tracks, begins at page 23. Types and Methods of Construction follow at page 37, the power house building at page 67, and the power plant, from coal pile to engine shafts, at page 77.
the-number-concept-its-origin-and-develo:
Levi Leonard Conant, a mathematics professor at Worcester Polytechnic Institute, wrote a study of how number ideas began and grew. The Macmillan Company published the book in New York and London. Conant looks at counting systems from many peoples rather than only the familiar decimal one.

Tables in the book give numeral words in Hebrew, Tahuatan, Bagrimma, Nahuatl, and other languages. Some systems count by fives, others by twenties, and the largest Nahuatl terms reach into the millions. By setting these systems side by side, Conant shows that counting is a human invention shaped by hands, trade, and custom, not a gift handed down in one form.
the-origin-and-permanent-value-of-the-ol: Charles Foster Kent, Woolsey Professor of Biblical Literature at Yale University, wrote The Origin and Permanent Value of the Old Testament. Only the contents are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. The list runs to sixteen chapters. It opens with The Eclipse and Rediscovery of the Old Testament. Later chapters treat the prophetic histories, the Hebrew sages and their proverbs, and the history of the Psalter. The formation of the canon and practical methods of study close the list.
the-pawns-count:
E. Phillips Oppenheim published The Pawns Count in 1918. A foreword lines up four voices: John Lutchester for England only, Nikasti for Japan only, Oscar Fischer for Germany first and America afterwards, and Pamela Van Teyl for America always. They were all right, the foreword says, except the German-American.

Chapter One opens in a fashionable London restaurant. Pamela, a beautiful American girl, points to a wall notice in French warning that enemy ears listen. Except for wounded companions, she says, it is the first thing in England that makes her realize the country is at war. A spy tale of the First World War begins over luncheon.
the-pianoforte-sonata-its-origin-and-dev: J. S. Shedlock's The Pianoforte Sonata traces the form in eleven chapters, published in London by Methuen and Co. Only the title page and contents appear here, so the chapter text is absent. The contents move from an opening chapter through Johann Kuhnau and his contemporary Bernardo Pasquini. Later chapters cover Emanuel Bach, Haydn and Mozart, and the men who came just before Beethoven. Closing chapters treat Beethoven, then Schumann, Chopin, Brahms, and Liszt, the sonata in England, and modern sonatas.
the-power-of-womanhood-or-mothers-and-so: Ellice Hopkins wrote The Power of Womanhood, or Mothers and Sons as a book for parents and those in a parent's place. E. P. Dutton and Company published it at New York, with an 1899 copyright. Hopkins is named as author of a life of James Hinton. What is shown here is the title page and the first page of the contents. Early chapters are headed Introductory, Why Should I Interfere?, First Principles, and The Secret and Method. Early Boyhood and Boyhood and School Life follow.
the-principles-of-scientific-management:
Frederick Winslow Taylor's Principles of Scientific Management, dated 1911, opens by quoting President Roosevelt: conservation of national resources is only preliminary to national efficiency. Forests vanish and coal and iron run out in plain sight, Taylor argues. The larger waste, of human effort through blundering and ill-directed work, leaves nothing visible behind. It calls for memory and imagination to grasp, though the daily loss exceeds the waste of materials.

No public agitation for greater efficiency has yet arisen, yet the need is widely felt. The search for competent men, from company presidents to household servants, was never more vigorous, and demand exceeds supply. What everyone seeks, Taylor says, is the ready-made competent man trained by someone else. The duty and opportunity lie instead in training men systematically.
the-professional-aunt:
Mary C. E. Wemyss's narrator in The Professional Aunt had her profession forced on her by her sisters-in-law and their children. Zerlina holds that one woman in every family should be a professional aunt, a post giving full scope to any reasonable woman's energies. An aunt who marries loses her perfecting at once, exchanging a fitted profession for a lottery. Zerlina's aunt must remember every nephew's and niece's birthday, which by her reasoning leads to presents.

The successful aunt also knows each child's particular taste, and the exact moment that taste changes. The narrator writes from Zerlina's point of view throughout this opening chapter. Professions, she observes, are often chosen for boys by parents, which is why shrewd boys become painters and artistic ones join the Stock Exchange. Her own calling came by family appointment rather than choice.
the-re-creation-of-brian-kent:
Harold Bell Wright frames his Ozark story with a long letter to his Auntie Sue, dated April 30, 1919, at Riverside, California. He teases her that she will deny ever living in a little log house by a river in the Ozark Mountains, then asks whether she is quite sure she never did.

Wright says he will be heartbroken if readers do not love her, and notes she will turn eighty-seven the next November. A verse from John Dyer about rivers running to the deep follows the letter. The dedication itself tells readers the book will treat an old woman's goodness as the center of a simple story of life and love.
the-regent:
Arnold Bennett calls his 1913 novel a Five Towns story of adventure in London. Edward Henry Machin walks home to Bleakridge at six minutes to six, reflecting that despite everything he does not feel so jolly after all.

Contents promise a dog-bite, a bank-note, entry into the theatrical world, titled hosts, a cornerstone, a first night, and a woman named Isabel. Bennett sends a provincial businessman into London theatre management, where money and art collide. The rueful opening mood promises comedy built on respectability shaken loose from home ground at last.
the-reminiscences-of-an-irish-land-agent: S. M. Hussey's reminiscences were compiled by Home Gordon and published at London by Duckworth in 1904 with two portraits. Contents move from ancestry, parentage, and education through farming and work as a land agent in Cork to famine and fever, then Fenianism. Here only the title pages and opening of the contents list are present, so the reminiscences themselves do not appear.
the-research-magnificent:
H. G. Wells published his novel in 1915, opening with a prelude on fear and aristocracy. William Porphyry Benham, readers learn, was led into adventure by an idea that possessed his imagination early and grew with him until it interwove with his whole being.

Benham had money enough to follow the idea around the world, into situations bordering on the fantastic that made him ridiculous and nearly sublime. Contents promise boyhood, town life, a wife named Amanda, a spirited honeymoon, and jealousy judged. Wells turns a life story into the biography of a ruling thought.
the-room-in-the-dragon-volant:
J. Sheridan LeFanu frames The Room in the Dragon Volant as a curious case. Its prologue says the case is referred to in an essay by Doctor Hesselius. That essay treats the drug lore of the Dark and Middle Ages.

Hesselius titled his essay Mortis Imago. He discussed the Vinum letiferum and the Beatifica. He also covered the Somnus Angelorum. About twenty other infusions and distillations appear in his list. Sages knew them eight hundred years earlier. Two of them, he alleges, remain known to a fraternity of thieves. Police-office inquiries sometimes support that claim, the prologue says. The frame promises a story where old drugs meet present crime.
the-russian-revolution-the-jugo-slav-mov:
Russian Revolution gathers pieces by four named writers. They are Alexander Petrunkevitch, Samuel Northrup, Harper Frank, and Alfred Golder. The volume also contains The Jugo-Slav Movement by Robert Joseph Kerner. The portion shown is Petrunkevitch's essay of March 18, 1918. Its subject is the role of intellectuals in Russia's liberating movement.

Petrunkevitch quotes a November interview with Leon Trotzky. He defended the Bolshevik coup in that interview. He claimed workers, soldiers, and peasants stood with the government. Petrunkevitch sets that claim against a private letter. His father Ivan wrote the letter in June. The elder Petrunkevitch had led the Constitutional Democrats in the first Duma. His son argues the Council was led by intellectuals. They were well educated men, unlike the masses they claimed to represent.
the-saint:
Antonio Fogazzaro's novel The Saint reached American readers under unusual circumstances, explained in a publisher's note dated New York, July 1906. The Congregation of the Index had condemned the book. The American publishers had secured Fogazzaro's sanction for their authorized translation before that sentence passed. As a loyal Catholic he could not have given it later. Once given, he did not feel justified in withdrawing it.

A further note prepares readers for the hero. Piero Maironi, the Saint, appeared in Fogazzaro's earlier romances. His wife was in a lunatic asylum. He had fallen in love with Jeanne Dessalle, a woman separated from her husband. A deathbed interview with his wife recalled him to faith and honour. He vanished from his friends after leaving a sealed paper with a priest. That paper described a prophetic vision behind his conversion.
the-stolen-white-elephant:
Mark Twain frames this comic tale as a curious history. A chance railway acquaintance told it to him. The man was an elderly official of the Indian civil service. Twain notes that the piece was left out of A Tramp Abroad. Doubts about its truth kept it out. The King of Siam, making reparation after a frontier dispute with Great Britain, sent the Queen a transcendentally royal present: a sacred white elephant.

The narrator conveyed the animal to Jersey City, where it was to recover its health before sailing. A fortnight later the elephant was stolen. The terrified official rushed to New York's detective headquarters. The celebrated Inspector Blunt was just leaving. The hunt launches Twain's satire on detective method and official fuss.
the-story-of-a-stuffed-elephant: Laura Lee Hope's Make Believe story of a stuffed elephant was published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, illustrated by Harry L. Smith, under a 1922 copyright. The pages present here hold the cover and title pages. The first line of a contents list follows. It opens with a chapter called The Elephant and the Mouse on page one. The elephant's own adventures do not appear.
the-strolling-saint: Rafael Sabatini's historical novel of 1913, reissued by Barnes and Noble in a 2011 edition, is presented here through its contents alone. The same contents appear in two companion records. They carry the book's fuller title, the confessions of Agostino D'Anguissola. A first book, The Oblate, leads off. Its chapters cover Gino Falcone and a pietistic thrall. Luisina, rebellion, and Fra Gervasio follow. A second book, Giuliana, opens at the house of Astorre Fifanti. Sabatini's narrative itself does not appear.
the-triumphs-of-euge-ne-valmont: Robert Barr's Triumphs of Eugène Valmont collects eight cases for his French detective. This record gives the contents list. A note says the attribution and table were added by the transcriber. Cases promise the mystery of the five hundred diamonds. They offer a bomb-thrower's Siamese twin and the clue of the silver spoons. Lord Chizelrigg's missing fortune, a ghost with a club-foot, and Lady Alicia's emeralds follow. An appendix adds two Sherlock Holmes parodies, Sherlaw Kombs among them. Valmont's own narration begins beyond these pages.
the-voyage-of-governor-phillip-to-botany:
John Stockdale published The Voyage of Governor Phillip to Botany Bay in London in 1789. The volume was compiled from authentic papers obtained from government departments. It adds the journals of Lieutenants Shortland, Watts, and Ball and Captain Marshall, with fifty-five copper plates and charts from actual surveys.

Stockdale dedicates the book to the Marquis of Salisbury, calling it everything so far known about the Sydney Cove settlement. Anecdotes of Governor Phillip follow, describing an officer who rose by merit like Drake, Dampier, and Cook. Phillip's father, Jacob, came from Frankfort and taught languages in England, while his mother, Elizabeth Breach, had first married a naval captain.
the-war-chief-of-the-six-nations-a-chron:
Louis Aubrey Wood chronicles Joseph Brant in The War Chief of the Six Nations, volume sixteen of the Chronicles of Canada. Published at Toronto in 1915, the book follows Brant from young Mohawk to statesman of the tribes. Contents chapters include the battle of Lake George, schooldays, Fort Stanwix and Oriskany, Cherry Valley, Minisink, and a final church bell.

Chapter one camps huntsmen along the Ohio river under moonlight, fires darting among the trees. Hunters strip prey and ready weapons while women move in the dancing shadows. One woman bends over a newborn infant and speaks his name into the still evening. Wood begins Brant's life inside the forest world his wars would shake, before England, school, and revolution divide his ways.
the-well-beloved-a-sketch-of-a-temperame:
Thomas Hardy calls The Well-Beloved a sketch of a temperament, and his preface describes its setting as a peninsula carved by time from a single stone. That isle has housed for centuries a distinct people with strange beliefs and singular customs, now mostly fading. Fancies grow there naturally, Hardy says, like soft-wooded plants that need sea air.

His hero is a native of natives who gives a name and continuity to a delicate dream common to all men, familiar already to Platonic philosophers. Hardy warns that verisimilitude is subordinated to this ideal, subjective aim. He also records the tale's history: serialised in 1892 under another title, it first appeared independently in 1897.
thoughts-on-religion-at-the-front: The Rev. Neville S. Talbot, assistant chaplain-general and late of the Rifle Brigade, wrote Thoughts on Religion at the Front. Macmillan published it in 1917 in London, New York, Toronto, and other cities. Talbot had been fellow and chaplain of Balliol and wrote The Mind of the Disciples. The edition was reprinted three times during 1917, in March, April, and November. The title and publication pages are what is shown in this record, so Talbot's front-line reflections themselves are not shown.
umboo-the-elephant: Howard R. Garis's Umboo, the Elephant belongs to his Circus Animal Stories, from the author of the Uncle Wiggily series. The contents follow Umboo from babyhood through fifteen chapters. He travels on the march, picks nuts, gets lost, meets a snake, and is caught in a trap. Later he goes to school, is sold, shipped, and at last reaches the circus. Only the title page and contents are present here, so Umboo's story itself does not appear.
un-doc-rio-declaration-on-environment-an:
World leaders at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro adopted this declaration, a short United Nations text of twenty-seven principles on environment and development. It came out of the largest gathering of heads of government held up to that time. Its aim was to link care for nature with the fight against poverty.

The principles say states may use their own resources but must not harm other states. They call for public access to information, action to cut poverty, and care that guards future generations. The declaration still frames talks on climate, forests, and fair growth today.
un-doc-yalta-conference-agreement:
Leaders of the United States, Britain, and the Soviet Union met at Yalta in February 1945 and produced this agreement on the postwar world. Franklin Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin bargained as the Second World War neared its end in Europe. Their choices shaped the map for decades.

The text covers the division of defeated Germany into zones of occupation. It sets terms for Poland, for war trials, and for Soviet entry into the war on Japan. It also confirms plans to found the United Nations. Few short texts carry more weight in modern history.
webster-s-seventh-of-march-speech-and-th:
Herbert Darling Foster studied Webster's Seventh of March Speech and the secession movement of 1850. His paper came from the American Historical Review of January 1922, with a foreword by Nathaniel Wright Stephenson. Stephenson marvels that so much of the history of the eighteen forties and fifties has slipped from general memory. Nine of ten Americans, he guesses, would strain to place that famous speech among the nation's political adventures.

He lists what an honest exam would demand. The Wilmot Proviso comes first, meant to make free soil of the land to be won in the Mexican War. The instant, bitter southern reaction follows. Plans to split the conquered ground between slave and free labor come next. The gold seekers of California in 1849 made a free state with no leave from Congress. Foster's study then takes up Webster's great compromise speech itself, and the storm it raised.
what-eight-million-women-want: Only the front pages are present here, so the chapters themselves do not appear. Rheta Childe Dorr published What Eight Million Women Want in 1910, for the members of the General Federation of Women's Clubs. The contents move from culture clubs to social service, then to women and the law. Later chapters take up factories, the servant question, and votes for women. Her pieces first ran in Hampton's Magazine. Readers see her full plan, chapter by chapter, but not the text.
with-british-guns-in-italy-a-tribute-to-: The pages here present the title page, dedications, and the start of a contents list for Hugh Dalton's With British Guns in Italy, first published in 1919, with no war narrative shown. Dalton had served as a lieutenant in the Royal Garrison Artillery. He gives the book to the cause of Anglo-Italian friendship. Quotes from Pericles' funeral speech and from Meredith head the work. The contents open with the Anglo-Italian tradition and Italy's part in the war. Twelve pictures and three maps aid the book.
with-wolfe-in-canada-the-winning-of-a-co:
G. A. Henty wrote this 1894 historical novel about the British fight for Canada. His preface tells young readers why the struggle mattered. England held only a narrow strip on the east coast. France held Canada, Louisiana, and a chain of forts between them. That wall shut English settlers out of the west.

The chapter list follows one hero through rescues, battles, and scouting. Named stops include Braddock's defeat, Lake George, Fort William Henry, Louisbourg, and Quebec. The final chapters cover the climb to the heights and the capture of Quebec under Wolfe. War history drives the plot throughout.
woman-suffrage-by-federal-constitutional:
Carrie Chapman Catt compiled this 1917 case for a federal voting amendment. The volume is dedicated to Congress and the state legislatures. Catt argues that no state should deny the vote because of sex. Her own chapter lists seven reasons for federal action. She notes that state constitutions can be nearly impossible to amend. Election fraud also goes unchecked, she says.

Mary Sumner Boyd's chapter then details recent defeats caused by legal technicalities. Other chapters gather testimony from supporters across public life. Readers get a campaign handbook, not a neutral history. Its goal was to win the amendment fight.
